claims.text: The Co-free FeNiCrMn alloy is initially a single-phase solid solution.
The FeNiCrMn alloy is produced by removing Co from equiatomic CoCrFeMnNi.
Removing Co reduces the stacking-fault energy of the alloy.
The reduced stacking-fault energy facilitates deformation-twin nucleation under dynamic loading.
Lower temperatures and higher strain rates enhance deformation twinning or near-twin defect formation in Co-free FeNiCrMn.
Deformation twins or twin-like defects increase dislocation storage.
Increased dislocation storage from twinning raises the strain-hardening rate.
Twin-mediated strain hardening helps maintain both strength and ductility in the Co-free alloy.
The equiatomic CoCrFeMnNi baseline has a higher stacking-fault energy than Co-free FeNiCrMn.
Under similar dynamic conditions, equiatomic CoCrFeMnNi deforms primarily by dislocation glide without substantial twinning.
Under identical dynamic loading, Co-free FeNiCrMn should develop a higher density of twins or related hexagonally ordered defects than CoCrFeMnNi.
Under identical dynamic loading, Co-free FeNiCrMn should exhibit a higher strain-hardening rate than CoCrFeMnNi.
Under identical dynamic loading, Co-free FeNiCrMn should maintain greater ductility than the Co-containing baseline.
Twin formation absorbs energy and beneficially shifts the yield strength and post-yield response of the Co-free alloy.
The proposed mechanism should be most prominent at low temperature and high strain rate.
Outside the low-temperature, high-strain-rate regime, the proposed twinning mechanism should be less evident.
A controlled comparison of Co-free FeNiCrMn and equiatomic CoCrFeMnNi across temperature and strain rate can test the proposed mechanism.
Failure to observe enhanced twinning together with improved strain hardening or ductility in the Co-free alloy would refute the hypothesis.
